opus-5.5.text:
I think the core issue is that people tend to imagine AI research as primarily a cognitive bottleneck, where if you just had more smart researchers thinking harder, progress would speed up dramatically. When you look at how progress has actually happened over the past decade or so, though, most of it has been driven by scaling up compute: compute for training runs, and also compute for experiments.

So suppose you automate the researchers. You now have millions of very capable AI researchers, but they're still sharing roughly the same pool of hardware. Every idea they want to test needs experiments, and the most informative experiments are often fairly large-scale, because many things that work at small scale don't transfer, and vice versa. You end up with a lot of cognitive labor competing for a fixed or slowly growing amount of compute. In economic terms, research labor and compute are complements, not substitutes. If you massively increase one input while holding the other roughly fixed, you get diminishing returns pretty quickly.

There's also the question of how much of past progress was "software" progress in the first place. Even algorithmic improvements are often discovered by running a lot of experiments, and some of them only become useful at larger compute scales. So software progress itself is partly downstream of hardware scaling. If you cut off the hardware scaling, you don't just lose the direct contribution of compute; you also slow down the algorithmic side.

The other piece is that compute scaling eventually runs into the real economy. To keep growing training compute at something like four or five times per year, you need more fabs, more chips, more energy, more data centers, and more capital. Those depend on physical buildout and on revenue to justify the investment. Automating AI research doesn't directly give you any of that. What would give you that is automating a much broader swath of the economy, so AI generates enough value to fund and physically build the next round of scaling.

So my view is that the story where you automate AI R&D, get a software-only intelligence explosion, and everything follows from there is less plausible than a story where AI progress is tightly coupled to broad economic deployment. I'm not saying automating research wouldn't help. It would help, potentially a lot. I just don't think it's sufficient on its own to sustain the current pace of progress once we start hitting limits on how fast we can scale compute, which I expect to start biting toward the end of the decade.

r001.rationale: The response says automating AI research alone is insufficient and that broader economic automation is needed to fund and build further compute scaling.

r002.rationale: It states that millions of automated researchers would compete for roughly the same compute, limiting experiments and producing diminishing returns.

r003.rationale: It links the expected compute limits toward the end of the decade to the need for AI to generate enough economic value to fund further scaling and avoid a slowdown.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that I don't think AI research is the bottleneck on AI progress to the degree that a lot of people assume. If you look at where the progress has actually come from over the past decade or so, a very large fraction of it is just compute scaling. You train bigger models on more data with more hardware, and you get better results. The algorithmic progress is real, and it's substantial, but a lot of it has historically been enabled by compute, in the sense that you need to be able to run experiments at scale to discover which ideas actually work. Ideas that look promising at small scale very often don't transfer.

So the picture where you automate the AI researcher and then progress just takes off assumes that what's scarce is researcher labor, and if you had a million copies of a good researcher, you'd be getting a million times the output. But if the real constraint is how many experiments you can run on a fixed amount of hardware, then having a million automated researchers doesn't help you nearly as much. They're all competing for the same cluster. You might get some gains from being smarter about which experiments to run, and I don't want to dismiss that, but there are diminishing returns there. You can't think your way to results you need the compute to verify.

And then on the compute side, the growth rate we've seen is not something that can continue indefinitely. Training compute has been growing something like four or five times per year, and that's been sustained by spending a rapidly increasing share of money and also by riding hardware improvements. Both of those have limits. You run into power constraints, fab capacity, the willingness of investors to keep putting in capital at that rate without seeing proportionate revenue. If compute growth slows later in the decade, which I think is plausible, then the question is whether software progress alone can compensate, and I'm skeptical it can, because software progress itself has depended on compute growth.

There's also a more subtle point, which is that the kind of research being automated matters. Automating the parts of AI research that are easy to automate, like writing boilerplate code or running sweeps, is useful but it's not where the hard progress comes from. The genuinely novel conceptual breakthroughs are rarer, and I'm not confident that current systems, or systems in the next few years, are going to be dramatically better at that than human researchers. They might be, but the evidence so far is more consistent with them being very good at accelerating the routine parts.

So when I put all that together, I think a model where you only automate AI research and expect that to carry rapid progress through 2030 is leaving out the fact that progress has been a joint product of labor, compute, and data, and you can't substitute one of those for the others without limit. If you want sustained rapid progress, I think you need the broader economy to be getting automated too, because that's what generates the revenue and the physical capacity to keep the compute scaling going.

r001.rationale: The response says sustained progress requires automating the broader economy as well as AI research, but does not specify much of the remotely performed economy.

r002.rationale: It says automated researchers would compete for the same fixed cluster, limiting the experiments they can run and the progress they can produce.

r003.rationale: It links revenue to continued compute investment and says broader automation could generate revenue, but does not clearly state that AI must produce substantial economic value by the end of the decade to avoid a slowdown.

astra-6.text:
I think the main distinction is between automating the labor that goes into AI research and automating the whole process of making progress. Even if you had AI systems that could come up with good ideas and write all the code, you would still need compute to run experiments and test those ideas. Making researchers much cheaper doesn’t automatically make that compute cheaper or more abundant.

Initially, you could get a lot of progress from exploring ideas that people haven’t had time to try. But as you increase the amount of research effort, you should expect other bottlenecks to become more important. Researchers might be waiting on experiments, or on a larger training run, or on new hardware. And building chips, data centers, and power infrastructure takes time.

So I’m not saying that automating AI research wouldn’t accelerate progress. It could accelerate it substantially. What I doubt is the inference that this alone gives you sustained, very rapid improvement through the end of the decade. For that, you need some account of how the other constraints get relaxed, or why algorithmic improvements remain sufficiently easy to find that you can keep making rapid progress despite those constraints.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes automating AI research labor from automating the whole progress process, but does not say this requires automating much of the remotely performed economy.

r002.rationale: It says that increasing research effort while compute remains constrained leads to experiment and hardware bottlenecks that limit sustained rapid progress.

r003.rationale: The response does not argue that AI must produce substantial economic value by the end of the decade to prevent progress from slowing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between automating the labor that goes into AI research and automating the whole process of making progress. Even if you had AI systems that could do everything a human researcher does, you would still need compute to run experiments, train models, and find out which ideas actually work.

If you suddenly make research labor much cheaper, you might get a substantial burst of progress. But that doesn’t necessarily translate into a permanently higher growth rate. You could just end up with lots of proposed experiments competing for the same limited compute budget. And increasing that budget requires chips, power, data centers—things that you can’t expand arbitrarily quickly just by having more intelligence available.

There’s also uncertainty about how much algorithmic progress is available and how difficult it becomes to find further improvements. Automating researchers doesn’t establish that each successive improvement will be as easy to discover as the previous one. You could have diminishing returns that absorb a lot of the additional research effort.

So I’m not saying automating AI research wouldn’t be a big deal. It could be a very big deal. I’m skeptical of the extra step where we assume that, once research is automated, rapid progress becomes self-sustaining through the end of the decade. That requires assumptions about the other bottlenecks and about the returns to research, beyond just the ability to automate the researchers.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether automated research alone can sustain progress, but does not say that automating research requires automating much of the remotely performed economy.

r002.rationale: It says more proposed experiments would compete for the same limited compute budget, constraining progress if compute does not expand.

r003.rationale: It discusses compute and research returns, but does not argue that AI must generate substantial economic value by decade’s end to avoid slower progress.
